Ryan Shenvi, PhD: The Shenvi lab studies chemical synthesis, focusing on complex "information-dense" molecules like natural products that are hard to make with existing tools. They develop new synthetic and computational methods (including density functional theory and neural network potentials) to predict how reactions will behave before running them in the lab, turning a handful of experiments into large sets of predicted outcomes and saving wet-lab time. They apply these tools to biomedical targets, notably kappa-opioid receptor ligands (salvinorin A, GB18) developed into selective, G protein-biased agonists, plus programs on 14-3-3 protein-client molecular glues, GABAa receptor antagonists, and species-selective SDH inhibitors. Their work aims to unlock faster routes to the branched, complex molecular frameworks found in drugs and materials, bridging fundamental chemistry with pharmaceutical discovery.
Supriya Srinivasan, PhD: The Srinivasan lab studies the gut-brain axis as a key regulator of metabolism, using the roundworm C. elegans as a genetically tractable model. They investigate how neuroendocrine and enteroendocrine signals let the intestine and nervous system communicate to control energy balance, feeding behavior, fat metabolism, and lifespan, focusing on how animals sense their internal state and respond via GPCRs, neuropeptides, and insulin-like signaling. Using large-scale genetic and small-molecule screens enabled by C. elegans's well-mapped neural circuitry, they uncover conserved molecular mechanisms. The lab has also extended into mammalian intestinal biology, examining how gut-derived signals affect fat mobilization, mucosal immunity, and inflammation—work relevant to obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and healthy aging.
Lisa Stowers Anderson, PhD: The Stowers lab is a neuroscience group studying how the brain detects and interprets odors and pheromones and turns them into behavior. Past work has shown that a specialized sensory organ (the vomeronasal organ) detects protein pheromone-like molecules to trigger defensive behavior between species, that urinary proteins involved in scent communication evolved differently across species, and that male pheromones can influence female reproductive development. More recent work aims to map a complete neural circuit in the mammalian brain connecting odor detection to behavior, and touches on interoception—how the brain senses signals from internal organs like the heart and stomach. Overall, the lab combines molecular, genetic, and circuit-level approaches to understand how the nervous system processes chemical and internal-body signals.
Andrew Su, PhD: The Su lab is a bioinformatics group that builds computational tools to organize and connect biomedical knowledge at scale. They develop widely used resources like the BioThings suite (MyGene.info, MyVariant.info, MyChem.info) and contribute to large knowledge graphs such as the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator, integrating data from hundreds of sources. Using statistics, computer science, and AI, they mine these datasets to generate testable hypotheses—for example identifying drug-repurposing opportunities and mapping drug mechanisms via their DrugMechDB resource. They collaborate with experimental scientists on single-cell transcriptomics, circadian biology, and infectious disease, and are increasingly exploring how AI agents and large language models can help scientists generate ideas and synthesize literature, with an emphasis on open, transparent, and reliable tools.
John Teijaro, PhD: The Teijaro lab studies viral immunology, using LCMV to model persistent viral infection and influenza virus to study acute viral disease in mice. They investigate how type 1 interferon signaling drives both the initiation/maintenance of persistent infection and the harmful cytokine amplification and immune pathology seen in influenza. Key findings include that endothelial (not epithelial) cells are central to cytokine amplification during flu infection, that blocking this amplification improves survival, and that blocking type 1 interferon signaling during persistent LCMV infection speeds viral clearance in a CD4 T cell-dependent way while restoring immune tissue structure. The lab also has a history studying memory CD4 T cells and tissue-resident immunity following influenza infection.
Luc Teyton, MD, PhD: The Teyton lab pursues two main lines of research. First, in response to rising antibiotic resistance, they develop therapeutic antibodies against bacterial and fungal glycans (surface sugar structures), using synthetic conjugate immunogens to generate high-affinity antibodies; this approach has shown proof-of-concept efficacy against Streptococcus pneumoniae and antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, guided by structural and synthetic chemistry studies. Second, for over 25 years they have studied how the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in type 1 diabetes, examining the normal relationship between the endocrine pancreas and immune system and how it breaks down. This work spans mice and humans, using modern genetics, immunology, stem-cell-derived islet organoids, and single-cell analysis, aiming toward clinical trials for prevention and treatment.
Eric Topol, MD: Eric Topol leads a research program at Scripps Research focused on translational and digital medicine. A practicing cardiologist, he directs the Scripps Research Translational Institute and is principal investigator on NIH grants supporting innovations to promote human health. His work explores how artificial intelligence can be applied to healthcare, including self-supervised learning methods in medicine, and he has written extensively on AI's role in making healthcare more human. His group is currently running a digital clinical trial testing a repurposed GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (already approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) for relief of long COVID symptoms, reflecting a broader focus on applying data-driven and AI-based approaches to real-world clinical problems.
Ali Torkamani, PhD: The Torkamani lab uses genomic and informatic technologies to identify the genetic causes and mechanisms behind human disease, aiming to define individual health risks and personalized interventions. Major focus areas include interpreting the human genome, discovering the genetics behind novel rare diseases, and building machine- and deep-learning models that predict risk for common diseases like coronary artery disease and pre-diabetes using genetic and wearable-sensor data. The lab also works on communicating genetically-informed disease risk to patients digitally. Their tools are being integrated into remote clinical trials that deliver personalized behavioral and therapeutic interventions, with the broader goal of using genomic data to help restore individuals to their personal baseline of health.
Renan V.H. de Carvalho, PhD: The Laboratory of Immune Longevity (LIL), led by Renan de Carvalho, studies what makes immune responses last a long time. Their top priority is understanding plasma cell longevity and what determines durable antibody (humoral) immunity—identifying why some immune responses produce lasting protection while others don't. Using transgenic mouse models combined with infection and immunization strategies, the lab investigates the underlying mechanisms of successful long-lived immunity. De Carvalho's prior work includes studies on immune evasion by Leishmania parasites and on how germinal centers (the sites where antibody-producing cells mature) are sustained after respiratory virus infection, giving the lab a background spanning infectious disease immunology and vaccine-relevant immune memory.
Julia Moore Vogel, PhD: The Moore Vogel lab conducts participant-centric health research and clinical trials aimed at complex, poorly understood illnesses, with a particular focus on long COVID. Rather than traditional in-clinic studies, they run decentralized trials using digital technologies, wearable sensors, and at-home biospecimen collection so people across the country and world can participate. As senior director of the All of Us Research Program, Julia Moore Vogel—who also lives with long COVID—directs research toward better symptom management and health equity for affected patients. One current study is testing a repurposed GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) for relief of long COVID symptoms.
Andrew Ward, PhD: The Ward lab uses integrative structural biology to study membrane proteins and viruses. They investigate membrane protein transporters, which move molecules into and out of cells, using x-ray crystallography, electron microscopy, and other biophysical techniques to uncover their largely unknown molecular mechanisms. A major focus is on viral surface proteins that mediate cell entry and how broadly neutralizing antibodies bind to and block viruses like HIV and influenza; using single-particle electron microscopy and electron tomography, they visualize antibody-virus complexes and whole viruses to understand how these antibodies work and to help design better vaccine immunogens capable of eliciting similar broad protection in humans.
Friedbert Weiss, PhD: The Weiss lab studies the neurobiology of drug and alcohol addiction, focusing on the brain circuits underlying motivation, reinforcement, and reward. Their research examines the neuropharmacology, neurocircuitry, and molecular basis of addiction, including how dependence and withdrawal develop, what drives drug craving and relapse, and how addiction impairs memory and cognitive function. Notable findings include identifying that cues associated with a single cocaine experience can trigger long-lasting drug-seeking behavior, and that the brain learns to seek alcohol for relief rather than just pleasure. Using animal models, the lab's work aims to inform better treatments for reducing cravings and relapse in people with substance use and alcohol use disorders.
James Williamson, PhD: The Williamson lab studies the structural biology of RNA and RNA-protein complexes. A core focus is ribosome assembly: using isotope pulse-chase mass spectrometry, single-molecule fluorescence, and time-resolved electron microscopy (with several collaborators), they measure the kinetics and cooperativity of ribosomal protein binding both in vitro and inside cells. They also study how RNA folds into 3D structures and is recognized by proteins, how RNA-binding proteins regulate stem cell differentiation in C. elegans germline development using x-ray crystallography, and how RNA-binding proteins control T-cell activation. Another line of work examines helicases involved in HIV replication, using biochemical and crystallographic methods to understand their role in transporting viral mRNA within infected cells.
Ian Wilson, PhD: The Wilson lab uses high-resolution x-ray crystal structures to understand how the immune system recognizes and neutralizes pathogens, aiming to inform vaccine design. They have solved over 250 structures of antibodies bound to diverse antigens, plus structures of T-cell receptors with MHC molecules and pattern-recognition receptors like Toll-like receptors, revealing how the immune system detects microbial threats. Much recent work focuses on HIV-1 and influenza: the lab has determined structures of rare broadly neutralizing antibodies against HIV-1's envelope proteins and against influenza hemagglutinin, identifying vulnerable sites on the viruses that can guide vaccine development, including for the 1918 flu strain and avian/swine influenza variants with pandemic potential.
